utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours; good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al., thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. Today is Wednesday. I would like to greet -- today is Tuesday. I would like to greet all the people present in the courtroom, Defence counsel, the accused, Mr. Scott, and Mr. Kruger, as well as Mr. Tomic, of course, who has been with us for a number of days now already. And I would also like to greet all those people who are assisting us. I would first of all like to ask the registrar to move into closed session for a few minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber, after Mr. Scott's cross-examination, discovered that --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There has been -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oral decision relating to the appearance of the expert witness of the Prlic Defence team Svetlana Radovanovic. On the 7th October 2008, the Prosecution filed a written submission requesting the Trial Chamber, inter alia, for it to cancel the testimony of expert witness Svetlana Radovanovic on the grounds that the Defence -- the Prlic Defence team had not as yet disclosed the expert report and the related exhibits. On the 20th of October, 2008, the Prlic Defence filed the expert report of Svetlana Radovanovic pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules. On 22nd of October, 2008, the Prosecution forwarded a letter to the Trial Chamber in which it informed it that it had read the report of Ms. Radovanovic but that the Prosecution was withdrawing its motion filed on the 7th of October, 2008. In addition, the Prosecution informed the Trial Chamber that it would be able to cross-examine Svetlana Radovanovic possibly in the week of the 24th of November, 2004, as has been planned in the most recent witness list or schedule provided by the Prlic Defence team on the 22nd of September, 2008. The Trial Chamber therefore acknowledges that the Prosecution has withdrawn its motion filed on the 7th of October, 2008, and rules that Svetlana Radovanovic will appear and come and testify as of the 20th of November, 2008, onwards. Mr. Scott, you have the floor for the rest of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, to all Your Honours. Sorry, I was just distracted looking at the transcript and I think there might be an issue so my apologies for being distracted. Good afternoon, Mr. President, all counsel, everyone in the courtroom who is helping us, each of Your Honours. Your Honour, just now in terms of scheduling, you'd indicated at one point that that there would be the possibility of the witness testifying the week of the 24th of November, and then at least it came out in translation that she would then be testifying on the 20th of November. So I'm not sure about the difference between the 24th and the 20th. Or at least that's how it came out on the record. Are you we talking about the 20th of November or the 24th of November? 20th, I believe, is in fact a Thursday, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, was it the 20th or the 24th? If the 20th is a Monday, he's coming on Monday the 20th; is that right? Or if the Monday is the 24th, then he would be coming on the 24th. I don't know. I don't have a calendar in front of me. You're the expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not an expert on these matters, but it is the 24th, which would be a Monday, and it's a woman, it's a she. We keep calling her a he, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the 24th is a Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Appreciate the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tomic. Just one -- I think maybe one question arising from our conversations yesterday before moving back to where we left off. When we were looking at the map of Mostar, as you will remember, and we were marking a number of locations, I think if I heard you correctly you said that at least for part of that time period when you were living at location 1 and 2 that -- with Mr. Prlic that there were two other persons who also lived at that same location, if you were sharing a flat or what have you, but just so we have that, could you tell us who the other persons were who shared the residence with you and Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While staying in my flat at location number 1, my friends were there, my friend's vehicle, Slavko Bevanda and Vidan Raspudic. And while staying at location number 2, the owner of the house, Mr. Dinko Slezak was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So at location number 1 there were four of you living in the house or flat, whichever it was, and then location number -- location number 2 there were the three of you, just to be very clear.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Sir, if we could then go back to the topic where we left off yesterday, and we were talking about some of the financial matters, and we were talking about the Bosnian dinar and the Croatian dinar, and we came to the point where I was going to ask you a couple of questions about the national bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, if I'm wrong please correct me, but my understanding is that the national bank, albeit in perhaps difficult circumstances, did continue to exist and operate throughout the war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I think you were shown two documents, and if -- if we can avoid looking at them it would maybe save everyone a bit of time and effort. You were shown two documents, 1D 01765 and 1D 01764, which were documents submitted to the national bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the purposes of obtaining permission, or I suppose one might call it a charter to open a bank, a Croatian bank in Mostar. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, I think you testified that it was necessary in order for that bank to legally -- the Croatian bank in Mostar to legally exist or operate it had to have a legal document from the national bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there was also documentation that was required in order for that bank to be I think you used the phrase acknowledged internationally. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, those permissions or that documentation was forthcoming; was it not? And based on that documentation a bank in Mostar was established; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just so we have it at this point in the record, as I said I'm always talking about dates, this series of documentation was being exchanged, if you will. Can you confirm that that was in November 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The decision was signed in November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving on the same topic but moving to June of 1993, I believe you were also shown a document which was marked 1D 01928 which was the application by the national bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina for a loan from the Prvedna Bank Zagreb for 100.000 Deutschmarks. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of the existence of that document but I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have it there in front of you now or at least on the screen? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So just going back, sir, to where we were -- to what we confirmed a few moments ago, again you will agree -- you do agree, don't you, that the bank continued to exist and operate throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The bank was in Sarajevo. However, the governor of the national bank was outside of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I think if we go back and look at the documentation, sir, the correspondence from that official comes -- comes out of Sarajevo. You're saying that's not correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document says Sarajevo, but the national bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina also had an office in Zagreb, and on and document in which money is being sent from Celje, the document that accompanied the first time that Bosnia and Herzegovina dinar was issued, in that document it said the national bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina Zagreb. So that was in November. As far as I know, Mr. Stijepo Andrijic, the then governor, did not later return to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well -- all right. Well, let's take a step at a time then just to be clear. So you're confirming that there was a national bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina which had a location in Sarajevo throughout the war, and you're saying that -- you're suggesting that there was also an operation of that bank in Zagreb, an office. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And in terms of -- and in terms of the locations and the documentation would you agree with me it would be best to look at whatever the documents themselves indicate? Or do you have a specific memory of those particular transactions?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember what happened in November, but the document before me is one I have only just seen. I can't comment on it. It says Sarajevo there, but as to whether it was drafted in Sarajevo or Zagreb, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going to -- back to the Bosnian dinar, I think that your testimony made it clear that the dinar continued to be used in various parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout -- throughout the war, and there were also -- there were also times that it was used in the area claimed to be part of Herceg-Bosna, and there were indeed times when the Herceg-Bosna government or authorities sent or provided BH dinars to HVO operations in Central Bosnia. Do I understand that correct -- all of that correctly?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the HVO HZ HB sent aid to Central Bosnia in the form of Bosnian and Herzegovinian dinars. That's what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the question to my answer -- the answer to my questions, excuse me, are yes, the dinar continued to be used in various parts of Bosnia during the war. It was also used in parts of Herzegovina or Herceg-Bosna from time to time and the HVO authorities in fact sent BH dinars into Central Bosnia. That's my question. All of that's true; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So there again, just so there's no confusion, the BH dinar at no point, at least during this time period, 1992, 1993, 1994, the BH dinar did not cease to exist and there was nothing about it that was -- I'm going to use the phrase there was nothing about it that was inherently dysfunctional. It may have been more widely used in some places than others, but it continued to exist and continued to be -- to be used in transactions in various parts of Bosnia throughout the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, for example, we were just talking about and it may be worth looking at one document as one of the examples that you were just talking about, sending dinars to Central Bosnia. Could you look, please, at 1D 02127, which will be in the Defence binder. 1D 02127. Now, that was a document, I believe, which showed that a number of dinars were being sent in to -- sent to Central Bosnia. Just a moment, please. Am I believe again -- I don't think there's anything controversial about that. You mentioned that the other day, and you again confirm that that in fact took place; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. This money was physically transported there as assistant -- as assistance to the municipal HVOs in Central Bosnia. There was no other way of doing it, no other financial transactions were possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So just again on this point about the dinar before moving to another topic. You weren't, you being the HVO HZ HB, I mean, you weren't sending your colleagues and friends in Central Bosnia, the municipal HVOs in Central Bosnia, you weren't sending them worthless money, were you? You were sending them something that had value and that they could use in conducting their affairs in that area; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that part of Bosnia and Herzegovina it was possible to use that money.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let's turn next to the -- to the German mark a bit more. If we can just agree on a few propositions I'll put to you, sir, and if -- I'll be grateful if you can answer these yes or no, if you can. I think they're all things you basically said, I think, in the course of your testimony before. The Deutschmark was widely used in Bosnia-Herzegovina as early as 1991, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I think according to a report prepared by Mr. Cvikl, the man that I asked you about yesterday, in his report he cites you to support the fact that in fact at that time the most widely used currency in Herceg-Bosna was the Deutschmark. Did he cite you correctly?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the period. There were periods during which the German mark was used the most. That was at the very beginning. And then the Croatian dinar was more present, and then when there was an absence of such money the German mark was used the most. That's why it was also used for official payment transactions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'm going to need you to help us as much as you can, please, with times and dates again as much -- as much as we can, because you just broke the use of the mark into about three different categories or times. You said in the very beginning the German mark was used the most. So when you say the very beginning, sir, can you give us approximately the time you're talking about, at least by year, for example?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about the time when this financial system in Yugoslavia broke up and the Bosnian and Herzegovinian currency that was set up, that was the end of 1991, the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The Bosnian currency had not yet been introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not sure where that leaves us sir, to be honest. I find it, at least as interpreted, a bit confused. You said in the very beginning the German mark was used the most. So are we talking about the period 1991, 1992? Please give us -- help us as much as you can.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period of time the German mark was the currency that citizens placed their faith in, and they tried to exchange the Yugoslav dinars that they had into German marks. That was why there was a black market.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let's try to keep it as simple as possible. All -- right now I'm just trying to get times and dates from you, not what they wanted to exchange on the black market, what this -- just dates. That's all I'm asking about. The Deutschmark, you said in the very beginning, and I just asked you, so are we talking -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps I should just explain what's happening. We are getting the files that we left in Courtroom III last night, which normally are brought with us to other courtrooms. This time it wasn't done, and that's what is happening here. Nothing mysterious about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think it's best, Your Honour, if I just pause until it's done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, again please, what I'd like you to assist us with now is just strictly dates. So when you said just a few minutes ago that this was in the very beginning, and I -- just if I can try to move us forward, that's what I'm trying to do, but also trying to give you an opportunity to be as clear as possible. I said were you talking about 1991/1992? So the answer to that question is either yes or it was some other time period, and if it was some other time period, please tell us exactly when it was.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that towards the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992 the German mark was something that people trusted, and that's why most of the payments were carried out against German marks, but companies at the time still operated with Yugoslav dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to tell you now because as you've learned, our time is limited, and I have to be unfortunately sometimes perhaps not as courteous as I would like to be, and when you answer the question I need to move on to another question. So my question now was not what companies did. We're talking about dates. Then you said there was a time when the Croatian dinar was used, and then the third period of time you said was that there wasn't enough currency or there were other issues involved and the Deutschmark once again became the dominant currency. So my question to you now is similar. Give us the dates for that. What was the time -- the dates for this third period when the Deutschmark once again became the dominant currency? And that's specifically my question, the dates.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the beginning of 1993. HZ HB regulations provided for the monies from non-resident accounts to be transferred onto the HZ HB accounts because the German mark became more present in all the transactions, and there was no need to convert German marks into Croatian dinars in the accounts in Croatia. You could receive monies and deposit monies into your foreign currency accounts in the HZ HB, i.e., you could deposit German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you testified last Tuesday also that in terms of value the Deutschmark was the most important currency in circulation in Herceg-Bosna; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The Deutschmark was certainly, would you agree with me, a more valuable -- both a more valuable and a more stable currency than the Croatian dinar?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And fairly soon after the Croatian dinar began to be more widely used in, I believe we just established roughly sometime in early 1992, mid-1992, it very quickly became subject to rapid inflation or devaluation; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And we might just -- we might just glance very quickly at Exhibit P 09255. P 0 -- yes. That will be in the second -- second binder. P 09255. And, sir, this is -- the cover sheet, if you will, the cover page is a compilation of information that has been taken from the business publications or newspapers that are attached in terms of exchange rates, et cetera. You'll see those behind, if anyone wants to look at those. But would you agree with me, and I certainly don't think you have this committed to memory, but would it seem to you about right that for example in January 1992 one Croatian dinar equalled 55 -- no, excuse me. My apologies. It was 55 Croatian dinars to the mark, and by the 27th of May, 1994, it was 3.716 Croatian dinar to the mark? Is that correct? Something like that.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe you said last Tuesday, and I think you maybe said it again just a few minutes ago, that the Deutschmark was used for payments between the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Herceg-Bosna during that time, during this period 1992, 1993, 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I think you also testified last Tuesday that during the conflict the international organisations, UNPROFOR, the humanitarian organisations, most of the international organisations and representatives who were on the ground in Bosnia-Herzegovina used the Deutschmark; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, sir, isn't it correct that ultimately it was essentially the Deutschmark at the end of the war that was -- or after the war that was in fact accepted as the new currency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and ultimately became known as the convertible mark, or KM? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the currencies that were present in Bosnia-Herzegovina were converted into the German mark first, and then the so-called convertible mark was introduced, and its rate of exchange was 1 to 1 against the German mark, the Deutschmark.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, sir, wouldn't it be fair to say throughout this period, from 1991 to its ultimate adoption, I believe it was in 1997 that the convertible mark was introduced, throughout that time period from a monetary perspective the Deutschmark always made more sense as a currency? It was more valuable. It represented the most value in transactions in the country. It was use by the internationals. It was more stable, subject to less inflation. It was by all measures superior to the Croatian dinar or the Bosnian dinar; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I come back, sir, to the question I put to you yesterday. Based on all that, would you agree with me that the selection or use of the Croatian dinar by Herceg-Bosna was not a function, a monetary analysis or monetary reasons, but it was essentially a political choice, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not a political choice. It was just a reflection of the reality, because the Croatian dinar had been present through the flow of goods and people from Croatia, and it penetrated all the way to Konjic, to Central Bosnia. It had its value, which obviously in this period here experienced devaluation, but it is seen from this that during the period when the German mark was re-established as the most -- the more important currency and when the Croatian dinar devaluated then it was the German marks that was the legal tender or, rather, the most present tender in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The next problem was the issue of notes and currencies. The smallest coin of one pfennig or five pfennigs did not exist, and that's where the Croatian dinar had a role to play as a transitional tender that was used in the territory of the HZ HB. And as I say, it was used only in one part of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the Republic of Croatia then adopted a currency called the kuna in May of 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And once again at that time Herceg-Bosna accepted the kuna as a currency to be used in Herceg-Bosna; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kuna replaced the Croatian dinar in monetary transactions. It looked differently and the name was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But once again, sir, you would agree with me, based on what you've just said, it was -- it was the Croatian currency, whatever it was, whether it was called the Croatian dinar, whether it was called the kuna, whatever the Croatian currency was, that's the currency that Herceg-Bosna wanted to use; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian currency was used in the territories of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I would like you next, please, look at -- it will be in the Defence binder, 1D 02148. And as you're looking at that, let me just ask you some introductory questions, if you will. During 1993, or the latter part of 1992 and continuing into 1993 since we see this document is dated the 2nd of February, 1993, how was Herceg-Bosna and the HVO meeting its needs for oil and petrol both for military and civilian purposes?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oil and petrol were obtained from the Energopetrol company based in Sarajevo before the war. It was in Sarajevo, and it had a business centre in Mostar, and that business centre moved its office first to Split, then to Ploce. In Ploce there was also a warehouse from which the area of the HZ HB was supplied. Before the war Ina had a large number of gas stations in the territory of the HZ HB, and Ina continued to supply these gas stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I already said that there were some private gas stations which continued their business operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, that apart from whatever deliveries were made on the -- on the coast, be it at Split or wherever in terms of tanker -- oil tankers, oil and petrol would be distributed throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time primarily then by tanker trucks, lorries; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if you look at this document which is -- comes from Mr. Prlic as president of the HVO HZ HB, this appears to be concerning an oil purchase, and I take it from the letter, and if you're looked at the letter, is it fair to say that this appears to be a transaction involving both the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Herceg-Bosna authorities? Is that right, that somehow this oil is being split, or am I misunderstanding the document?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said I was present at a meeting in Zagreb in the office of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina together with the head of the department -- the department for economy, who expressed the need for one part of the oil and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I apologise. So the answer to my question is yes. Now -- and so was the oil divided between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Herceg-Bosna in some fashion? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then what I take this letter to be the further details to be of the 50 per cent of the oil -- of the available -- it says of the available quantity. Fifty per cent of that was being distributed to the department of defence of the HVO HZ HB, and then on down through the rest of the numbers. So this is how the Herceg-Bosna's share, if you will, was then being apportioned out as reflected in the letter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was this a unique transaction, or did you see or were you aware of similar transactions in 1992, early 1993?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the implementation of the Zagreb agreement is reflected in this document, and I don't remember any other such transactions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This was a one-time deal. Is that -- is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was a one-off, just a one-time deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Now, sir, we saw a few moments ago, and you can -- and you talked about it again last week, that we saw that the national bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina was involved in approving the establishment of the Croatian bank in Mostar. We talked about that again already this afternoon. You also testified last week that the HVO was able to obtain the needed SDK software from the director of the SDK office in Sarajevo, and now we've seen an example of a transaction being conducted with the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I put it to you, sir, that it appears that whenever it suited the HVO they could have and did have contact and dealings with the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo or elsewhere. They could get the software. They could get the necessary approval to open a bank. They could make arrangements to purchase oil. They could do all those things, but on the other hand, when it suits you or when it suits others, were told that the BH army was "cut off." Now, was -- isn't that correct, sir? Isn't this a moving target? It's on one hand whenever it's convenient Sarajevo was cut off, the BiH government is cut off, but on the other hand whenever you need it for something, it's always there?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One cannot really put it that way. These were just individual activities which did not represent the functioning of the system, i.e., the government. What this boils down to are decisions that were implemented individually by people who left Sarajevo or dealt with the issues of that sort in Zagreb. In other words, there was no communication in the sense that institutions of the system could function like that. The governor of the Central Bank would use a customary procedure according to which he should have received a request from the regional office of the Central Bank that existed in Mostar before the war. However, there was no longer a regional office which would -- which could file a request, nor could that document be sent to Sarajevo. It should have complied with all the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina and deliver to -- delivered to the Central Bank governor who would then issue his decision. What we're talking about here are individual arrangements and deals and not about the functioning of the government and the organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that's the context I would like to put this in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Individual transactions and deals add up to lots of individual transactions and deals, sir. And let me about on to communications. Let me put a similar question to you. You've said that the communications with Central Bosnia were cut off, but I have to tell you, sir, and I think it's fair for me to do so, that this Chamber in the last two and a half years has seen or heard about hundreds of communications between Mostar and Central Bosnia in 1992 and 1993. Now, how does that fit in with your assertion that communications with Central Bosnia were cut off?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about the financial sector which was my purview. We used telecommunications as the customary way of functioning in payment transactions and in the bankers' system. However, that did not function. Those communications were interrupted. There were only the type of communication of physical nature. A person could come from Central Bosnia and go somewhere, and that's what we did. Central Bosnia functioned in payment transactions, as did Posavina. That was isolated as an island. And then we would do our accountancy between these two islands, and the physical difference in the money was transferred from one part to another which largely depended on the balance that had to be covered. When I say communication, I mean the electronic communications which are indispensable for the implementation and the functioning of payment transactions and bankers' system.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I appreciate that, sir. I'm talking to you now and I'm asking you about the questions that I'm putting to you are not limited to banking -- electronic banking transactions. And I'm putting to you, sir, that isn't it correct that your position on Central Bosnia being cut off in terms of communications really a bit like your position on the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina being cut off? It's cut off when it suits you and it's not cut off when this doesn't suit you. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the form of the question. How does one answer this question, Your Honours? In which sense? How can the gentleman be allowed -- be asked to answer this question. Look at the question as it's framed. It's unfair to the witness, and it really gets us nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me rephrase -- let me come at it differently then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me come at a differently. And I don't need any comments from counsel. I'll try to do the best job I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's come at it from the other way. If Central Bosnia was cut off, sir, then I suppose that none of the territories that supposedly belonged to Herceg-Bosna in Central Bosnia, Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, Vares, those were likewise really -- really they weren't part of Herceg-Bosna, because they were cut off. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again I'm going to object to the form of the question. He was talking about cutting off in the sense from his perspective dealing with finances. He also talked about how money would be transferred physically from one place to the other. So this term "cut off," the way it's being use by the Prosecution is -- is not properly being used in the same way as the gentleman. Also, look at the type of question that he's framing. How does one answer this question? Again, it's vague, it's unclear, it's ill phrased, and perhaps he may want to take another shot at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, it seems that when you say "cut off," the witness seems to say something else and understands something else than cut off. So ask him whether according to him Central Bosnia was totally isolated from the rest in terms of telephone communication, transfer of -- financial transfer, goods transferred, so forth, so whether being isolated or cut off meant that there was no financial link between Central Bosnia and Mostar or Sarajevo but that on the other hand, circulation was possible. Try to get him to be more specific. I believe that maybe we have an ambiguity between the -- what you understand and what the witness understands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll try. I would just like to just very briefly respond to the objection just so that the record is clear and perhaps to the extent may assist the Judges. Your Honour, I submit to the Chamber that in the last two and a half years the Chamber has heard that term used extensively, including by the Defence. Sarajevo was cut off. Central Bosnia was cut off. And I think everyone in the courtroom knows what that means. It's not a term that I just invented today. Secondly, I was very clear in my question to the witness, and I was trying to assist the witness to say that he may have been talking about electronic banking transactions but that's not what I'm talking about, and I'm asking the questions, with due respect. So I'm asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not talking about electronic banking transactions, I'm talking about communications more broadly. And if I could pick up on a word the President just suggested, is it your position that Central Bosnia was isolated in the sense of no dealings, no communications, not just electronic banking transactions, but it was isolated? There wasn't exchange of people, there wasn't exchange of goods, there wasn't exchange of currency? What was it? Or not? Or in fact, sir, isn't it a fact that it was not isolated, that it was not isolated in the way that some would like the Judges to believe.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were moments and periods during which it was impossible to even physically go to Central Bosnia. There were such moments when you could not even physically go there during the conflicts. I know that in order to carry out any financial transactions, to execute payment orders, even HVO helicopters had to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's go now to -- unless the Court has -- Judges have questions, I'll change topics. Sir, I'd like to talk to you now a bit about the customs system and the border operations that you have testified about, and again I'd like to see if I understand you correctly, and we can have a base on which to go forward. As I understand your testimony, sir, you agree that Herceg-Bosna and the HVO authorities in 1992 and 1993, at least, perhaps also thereafter but at least during that time, established a customs system and conducted border operations primarily on the border with the Republic of Croatia, and in doing so Herceg-Bosna collected various revenues. Are we in agreement on that?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I also understood you to say last week that you recognise that such things as operating a customs system and conducting border operations, those are functions that we normally associate and that you, sir, would normally associate with being conducted by a state; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I further understood your testimony to be that at least some, if not all of the customs and border-related revenues that were collected by Herceg-Bosna, some or all of that money should have been in fact sent to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina as part of its general budget revenues and then to be reallocated and apportioned as part of the budget process. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said. I mentioned that it was normal procedure. That's how the customs administration of a state functions. Under normal circumstances the money goes to the budget, and then from the republic's budget needs financed in accordance with the various items on the budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I understand that that didn't happen in the sense, and what I mean by that is the revenues collected by Herceg-Bosna as a result of the customs and border operations, those monies were not, during the period 1992, 1993, 1994, those monies were not in fact sent on to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the money from customs, from duty imposed on goods arriving in the area of Herceg-Bosna was sent to the budget of the HZ HB, paid into that budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is no, the monies were not sent to the BH government; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as I understand your testimony, the reason that you gave for that was -- I think we're back to this notion that there wasn't a means to do so. Sarajevo was cut off or isolated, and the means didn't exist to make these payments which otherwise should have been made. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We saw a document at one point that said that Herceg-Bosna, the HZ HB Presidency, was refusing to accept or, if I can say, take on board any financial obligations or debt incurred by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina unless some way that debt was directly linked to providing some benefit to Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a decision according to which it would be accepted if one-third was to be directed to the territory of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And which actually leads me to my question. Where did the one-third come from, and what was that based on?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was a decision of the Presidency of the HZ HB. I don't know. I assume that it had to do with -- I don't know, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And can we agree, though, sir, if we apply that same principle and if we're going to be objective and neutral about it and we're going to apply that same principle, then two-thirds of all the revenues and taxes and monies collected by Herceg-Bosna, the HVO, should have been sent on to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. We're dealing with taking out loans with the debts of the state, and representatives of the HZ HB didn't participate in this and they didn't know what the intention of these funds was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm applying the principle a bit more broadly because you said -- we established a few minutes ago and you said, you agreed with me, as you testified last week, that when Herceg-Bosna was conducting these customs operations and generating revenue, you agreed that that money should have gone to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then we talked about this principle of one-third. And I'm just saying if you apply that principle fairly, would you not have to say that any other revenues and monies collected by Herceg-Bosna, be it taxes, be it levies, be it fees, two-thirds of that money should go to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina; correct? Or it was a one-way street, is that what you're telling the Judges? You could keep your money, Herceg-Bosna could keep its money, but on top of that it expected to get money from the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're dealing with two types of revenue, and you cannot make such analogy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to 1D 02744 in the Defence binder. Do you have 1D, sir, 02744? Again, this is a document that we've already discussed about, so I'm not showing you something you haven't seen before. This concerned a salt transaction, the purchase -- the purchase of salt in December 1992. Excuse me a moment, please. And I just wanted to understand a bit better about, again, some of the things you talked about last week in terms of some of the financial aspects. If we look at the second page under "Payment Method," or wherever you find that in the duty, sir. The first method of payment apparently was the transfer, what appears to be a -- what we've been calling an electronic funds transfer to a bank account in Croatia at the Zagrebacka Banka denominated in Croatian dinars; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can we -- based on what you were telling us last week, can we understand from that that somehow apparently there was the means for this purchaser, in paying for this transaction, to pay for the salt had the means of making an electronic transfer involving a bank in Croatia? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then the second method of payment we see is in Bosnian dinars to go to giro account, and then there's a number at the Tuzla SDK, and I believe you touched on that last week but I just wanted to see if I understand. So at some link in the chain of these transactions, and we're going to talk about that for a moment, but somewhere in this link of transactions, series of transactions, there was an electronic link or what you've called an SDK link that was operating; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we have a typical contract, and it's true that 30 per cent could be paid in Croatian dinars into a resident account. Buyers also had non-resident accounts and they could perform such transactions from one account to another in Croatia. Fifty per cent in BH dinars where it says quite precisely through the SDK branch in Zenica or other branches that deal with payment transactions with the SDK Tuzla branch. So this shows that in Bosnia and Herzegovina the branches don't have anything to do with the branches in Tuzla. It's Zenica that has a link to the Tuzla branch or other branches in the Tuzla area that communicated with Tuzla. That is why the second paragraph says that if the buyer had money in an account in Zenica he could pay in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just trying to confirm that that was -- I understand it correctly. So there was an electronic transactions link between -- apparently between Zenica and Tuzla. We're clear on that; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I take it then from what you've said over the last few minutes that in order to get the money to Zenica before it could then be transferred electronically on to Tuzla, the money would have to get to Zenica some other way. Do you know how money -- this money would have been communicated to Zenica in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The money could only be physically transported, which wasn't a good idea, given the way one had to travel. So most of the payments were made by paying sums of money into non-resident accounts abroad. And here we -- in this case cash was paid in by the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on looking at this type of contract, you're saying that this is a standard contract. Seen from the outside, one has the feeling that three currencies are being used, the Croatian dinar, the BH dinar, and the Deutschmark. The three currencies are used on the basis of 30 per cent, 50 per cent, and 20 per cent. That's a ratio. So were these widely circulated contracts when such transactions were made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because -- well, part was paid in Croatian dinars, because the company would buy goods for that money because transport costs were at a minimum then. It was for their workers. Fifty per cent was in BH dinars so that workers in Tuzla could be paid their salaries and so that they could cover their expenses that were paid in dinars in the municipality of Tuzla. As for German marks, these marks were used to obtain goods from outside Croatia, goods that they needed to operate. So this is how companies tried to maintain the value that they had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And in fact, you finished the remaining questions I had on that particular document. So I'll move on to another item unless the other Judges have questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in addition to that transaction, we also discussed last week, and it actually was mentioned a few minutes ago or earlier today, the transfer of Bosnian dinar to the central Bosnian municipal HVOs, and we looked at I think in the course of last week several examples of that. I think there was at least one in January of 1993 and at least another one in March of 1993. And I don't know that we really need to look at the documents, to take the time to do that. In one instance, for example, there were 3 billion dinars. There was the approval by the HVO HZ HB to convey or provide 3 billion BH dinars to the Central Bosnia HVO. And how would this -- how were the dinars then transported to the Central Bosnia HVOs, or provided I guess. To say transported perhaps gives the answer, but how were they going to be provided and put in the hands, if you will, of the municipal HVOs in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Authorised officials from municipal HVOs would come under escort, a police escort usually, and take over from the treasuries of the SDK in Posusje or Siroki Brijeg the money in question. They would then transport that money to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And let me next direct your attention to similar situations where Croatian dinars were provided to locations in Central Bosnia. Again I'm not going to take the time to go to the particular documents, but we looked at two instances -- we saw two instances of that last week at least. For the record, one was reflected in 1D 02114. Another one was reflected in Exhibit 1D 02137. I think in the first one there was a transfer of 5 million dinars to the HVO Sarajevo. And my question to you, sir, is the same. In what way were 5 million Croatian dinars put in the hands of the HVO Sarajevo in March 1993?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Sarajevo HVO -- or, rather, the authorised officials physically received that money. They received that money themselves, then made use of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again going back to one of our themes for the day, if Sarajevo was cut off or isolated, how did you get the 3 million Croatian -- 5 million Croatian dinar to the people in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually the money was used to buy goods, and this is how the population of Sarajevo was assisted. The goods were then transported by convoy in the same way that other goods entered Sarajevo, because Croatian dinars couldn't be used in Sarajevo to buy anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, it appears from the documents, and it may, if it assists us, we made need to look at the document, but it appears from 1D 02114 this was the approval to send 5 million Croatian dinars to HVO Sarajevo. This is the decision on monetary assistance to be granted to the HVO municipality. And at least on the face of the document, sir, it appears that it is currency, it is money, it is dinars that is being provided. Now, do you know for a fact that was not the case?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I haven't understood your question. The 5 million, that was a decision taken, and that money was handed over to the HVO representatives of Sarajevo municipality in person, because it was impossible to forward that money electronically.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How did these people get from Sarajevo to pick up and collect the 5 million Croatian dinar?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of the official representatives -- one official representative managed to leave Sarajevo, and this official picked up the money and then had that money at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tomic, there's something I don't understand. If somebody comes from Sarajevo to pick up these 5 million Croatian dinars and goes back to Sarajevo with these dinars - we are now talking about March, 1993 - you said a few moments ago that one could not use this money in Sarajevo because it was not the legal currency, so to speak. What is the point of bringing in money which cannot be used? That's what I'm trying to figure out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you haven't fully understood me. They received 5 million Croatian dinars, and they used this money to buy goods. They turned the money into goods. It was possible to go to Sarajevo through the tunnel or over the airport strip and in such cases they joined convoys and entered Sarajevo with goods, not with Croatian dinars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, if I have understood you correctly, those's 5 million Croatian dinars were used to pay for goods that entered Sarajevo either through the tunnel or through another route. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A few more minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, sir. And let me turn to another topic which actually relates -- well, maybe it does. We'll see. We've been told at various points in the trial that the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina had certain logistics offices or in fact that the government had certain offices in Zagreb. Is that correct? Are you aware of that as well?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I take it these logistics offices in Zagreb were for the purpose, at least for a time, of again buying -- buying materials, whatever they were, and getting those materials in some fashion to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know where these offices located in Zagreb and perhaps other parts of Croatia, where did they get the funds in order to conduct their business to pay for these transactions, to pay for goods?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was in Senoje street in Zagreb. At least when I was at the meeting it was located in that street. As to how they were financed, well, that was an issue for the then government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which used accounts in Croatia and other countries in order to buy goods and in order to cover the expenses of their operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the banks that Herceg-Bosna used also had both, I take it, electronic and physical means of communication with Zagreb; is that correct? Banks in Split, banks on the border between, for example, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, these are all banks that had banking relationships or the ability to conduct banking transactions in Zagreb and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The banks in Croatia are included in the network, and it was possible for them to make payments to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Which brings us back, sir, to this point, and that is if in fact, as you've told us, Herceg-Bosna was collecting this customs revenue and border-related revenue and collected it, and if, as you say, you recognised that was a state function, and if, as you say, that money should have been paid to the Bosnia-Herzegovina but according to you, there was no means to do so, couldn't it have been transferred to these banks in Zagreb where both the bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the government accounts or Herceg-Bosna accounts and which that money could have been transferred if Herceg-Bosna had really wanted to pay that money?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, technically speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the fact that the money wasn't paid wasn't due to a lack of means, sir, it was due to a political decision. Herceg-Bosna was not about to send that money on to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it had nothing to do with the lack of means to do so; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You've just told us that there were ways of conducting transactions between Croatia, between Herceg-Bosna --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object. The gentleman was about to explain his answer, now he's entitled to explain, even under cross-examination, even -- if the answer requires an explanation, he's entitled to do so. Look at the question. Look at the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I won't intervene further, Your Honour, except I think it was Mr. Karnavas who said I don't know how many umpteen times yes, no, I don't know, was the appropriate answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But in any event, go ahead he, sir. Go ahead and tell us why it is, why it is you -- Herceg-Bosna and the HVO authorities couldn't make payments, couldn't transfer money to accounts or representatives of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina if they had wanted to.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time that this was happening, at the time this financial system was being set up, it was a key issue in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The key issue was the issue of defence, and the HVO was a part of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this money was used for defence. And at a meeting that we had with Mr. Izetbegovic in Mostar towards the end of 1992, this issue wasn't even openly discussed. We explained that we had to establish supervision over the goods entering Bosnia and Herzegovina, establish borders, et cetera. We said we were following republican instructions and applying them to the extent it was possible in the area of the HZ HB. We said this was a matter of priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I note, Your Honours, before the break we can finish on this point, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All that being as it may, sir, what we've come to -- would you agree with me that the conclusion that we've come -- the point we've come to is that the non-payment of these fees, the fact that Herceg-Bosna did not pay or send on this money to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina had nothing to do with the lack of means to do so? Correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with you only partly. At that time we did not receive any information from Sarajevo about any accounts, where they were, what accounts belonged to the budget, what accounts belonged to the customs, tax authorities, and others. Those were the accounts that were mostly used for assistance and the procurement of goods and defence supplies by the government in Sarajevo, and we were not in a position to know what accounts those were, and there was no way for us to be able to pay any money into those accounts. We learned about these accounts much more through the transactions that you have just shown me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You didn't -- you didn't think to ask some of these representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina, "Oh, by the way, where are your bank accounts and what are the account numbers? We'd like to send you some money." When you met with Izetbegovic in Zagreb, when you met with Izetbegovic in Geneva and other places and other representatives of the Bosnian government, did Mr. Boban or did Mr. Susak or Mr. Tudjman or anyone say, "By the way, we'd like to send you some money because we owe it to you. Where should we send it?" Or you were just -- you were happy to just keep the money and not say anything more about it? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me tell you that I never participated in any political negotiations or meetings except for the meeting with Mr. Izetbegovic when he came to Mostar. I've told you that the contact that we had with the government or the office of the government in Zagreb is another one, and no account numbers were given to me. We were not given any possibility to pay money. We were only talking about using the external aid that arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's all that we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a quarter to 4.00, and we will have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, staying on the topic of customs and border-related revenues, if we could go forward, didn't this same situation in fact exist in 19 -- even by 1995, where Herceg-Bosna was collecting this revenue and not providing any of it to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995 an agreement was reached about the complete separation of revenues within the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina between the areas under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the areas under the control of the HVO. And this was done because of the purposeful utilisation of the budget in the areas, and the key was in the establishment of a federal budget and unique system of payment transactions, and then the two budgets were merged and the revenues from the customs duties collected were then channeled into the revenue of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you please look at Exhibit P 10683 which should be in binder number 3. Binder 3, P 10683. This is something called a VIP Daily News Report, and while there is a date on the top -- for the top of the first page under the letterhead, if you will, of October 17th, 2008, you'll see in the footer of the document that the document is actually dated 23 January 1995. If I might just indicate that the October 17, 2008 date seems to be a function of when it's accessed on the computer, on the internet. But if you look, sir, at the --it will be on the second page of the English version, but there is a section that is -- gives a report about this issue of customs revenue in which it is reported that Neven Tomic said the federation's entire customs income would go only to Herceg-Bosna, although the federation parliament adopted a common customs law last week in Sarajevo. It's also indicated in this article that Croat authorities were collecting 1 million Deutschmarks in customs duties every day at the Doljani border crossing from Croatia to Bosnia. Is all of that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A federal law was indeed passed. However, no federal budget was passed, and it was never said how the institutions of the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be funded. The biggest pressure was for the revenues that were collected in the territory of the HZ HB to be channeled into the budget in Sarajevo. However, the federal army was still not established. The federal pension fund was still non-existent. In other words, the beneficiaries of the budget had still not been established, and by the agreement within the Minister of Finance Mr. Kreso and myself, it was clearly defined that in the transitional period before these institutions were established, the revenues that were collected for which the end user was the importers in the HZ HB should remain in the HZ HB. As for the revenues that were channeled towards the areas under the control of the BH army would then be channeled into the budget of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that the Croat authorities, the Herceg-Bosna authorities around this time were in fact collecting approximately 1 million Deutschmarks in customs duties every day at the Doljani border crossing?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. The Doljani border crossing was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... P 10685.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. My learned friend may wish to explain the document that we have just seen in front of us, the VIP Daily News Report. The English and the Croatian versions were shown, but they're not one and the same text, and it's very hard to tell what the original is, whether the original is English translated into Croatian or vice versa. Both bear the number 403. However, the dates are different. 23 January 1995 in Croatian and 18 October in English. And when you look at the contents, you will see that the two versions do not correspond to each other. The sequence is different, and not all the articles are in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, in Kovacic found out that the English text dates -- one text is January 23, 1995, whereas the other one is 17 October 2008 depending on the language. Could you shed some light on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe that the original publication is an English publication. I may be wrong on that. At least that's the -- well, I think that's the case. I can't swear to that, to be honest. It looks to me like having seen translations for the past ten years here, it appears that the document attached in the Croatian language is a prepared translation. As to the date, I thought I was trying to preempt that question by explaining that this document was downloaded from the internet. Perhaps other people in the courtroom have experienced that sometimes whenever you download something from the internet you get a date of download or date of printing as an electronic function. The footer of the article in the English version and in -- is January 23, 1995, and we submit that the date of the publication is that date, the 23rd of January, 1995. It certainly wasn't a few weeks ago in 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm grateful for this explanation. However, I'm still confused. In the translation, i.e., in the Croatian text, the title of the first article is the same as in the English version, "Contact Group in Pale, in Sarajevo," which translates into the same thing in Croatian. However, when you read the article itself, the contents do -- are different, as if the two sets of materials have been mixed up. In the English version there is no reference to Karadzic, Tomas who are mentioned in here. This is something I can't see in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is. Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Maybe I have a wrong copy. Maybe my binders got mixed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could go on to Exhibit 10685. So this is another article apparently from the Ljubljana Oslobodjenje dated the 20th of April, 1995. So it's about four months, approximately four months later than the first article. And it appears in this article that in fact the same situation continues to exist. Federal -- title "Federal Partners In Conflict Over Customs." In the first paragraph: "The decree on temporary measures for the importation and trade in products adopted by authorities operating on territory under the control of the HVO ... does not confirm to federal regulations and is causing consequences for the entire territory of the federation." Now, wasn't this same thing going on, sir, in -- in 1994, 1995? It might have been resolved at some point but for a substantial period of time Herceg-Bosna continued to collect and keep all the customs revenue; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Before the gentleman answers the question, we don't have the original version in the B/C/S. I guess Ljubljana must be a Slovenian-Croat version, or Slovenian-Yugoslav, whatever. So perhaps the gentleman should be given the opportunity to look at the original version before he can comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If it's not in the binders, Your Honour, it may be -- if it's not in the binder, Your Honour, then there hasn't -- a translation has not yet been obtained. I can put -- I can certainly read to Mr. Tomic any relevant portions of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The point, sir, is wasn't this an ongoing issue and what I just said is true, whether you see it in this article, can you just confirm to the Judges that during this period, 1994, 1995, Herceg-Bosna was continuing to collect and keep all the customs revenue?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a text from Oslobodjenje which was not a Slovenian paper. Oslobodjenje was a Sarajevo-based newspaper which was printed during the war, and during that period of time it was printed in Ljubljana. Throughout all the period after the Washington Agreement of which I've already testified, the approach to the implementation of the Washington Agreement on the part of the Bosniak partners in the government was to simply have the institutions of Herceg-Bosna abolished and join the work of the republican institutions which had hitherto functioned in the territories under the control of the BH army. According to the Washington Agreement we were supposed to build new institutions. In that period, the package of the laws to regulate new institutions was not adopted. Who were the beneficiaries of the budget? This was not established, and this was the subject of a major pressure exerted by the Bosniak side through the Sarajevo media, and what they were saying was not the truth. The border crossing Doljani that I just mentioned a while ago was the least-used border crossing which is reflected in the budgetary revenues of the HZ HB, and as a result of this the situation that we ended up with --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in the next-to-last paragraph of the article it says this, and if you don't have it in your own -- I have the impression perhaps you can read English, but be that as it may, it can be translate to you. In the article it says: "Herceg-Bosna is constantly finding new forms of financing that are not controllable." Wasn't Herceg-Bosna and the HDZ throughout this period doing everything possible to obstruct the establishment and the working of the federation?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Incorrect. We insisted on the establishment of new federal institutions, and that was the fundamental cause of the slowness in procedure and the functioning of the government and federation within the same package. When the agreement was signed on the implementation of the federation before the Dayton in 1995, and when only the government of the federation was established and where -- and also the government of the republic as a separate government, then the functioning and the merger of the territories under the control of the BH army and the HVO respectively started because new institutions were being established and introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just -- just for a point of clarification, Your Honours, this is a quoted part that was quoted in the question. This is from a Hasan Muratovic. So it's not that the article is saying it. This is what this gentleman claims, at least in this particular article, which I find rather interesting because it says Ljubljana not Sarajevo Oslobodjenje. And it also talks -- it says something about Serbo-Croatian. By this point the Muslims have their own language, which is Bosniak or Bosnian, depending whether it's the federation or the Dayton Accords. So I find it rather interesting that they're going back to Serbo-Croatian after all that bellyaching that they didn't have a language. So if this is in 1995, this is printed in some place other than Sarajevo. We don't have the original version. I find this rather suspect. And now we're quoting from it and we're not saying we're quoting from Dr. Hasan Muratovic, but rather, we're saying this is what is in the article as if somebody did actual research. So I would suggest, Your Honours, given that there is a lack of foundation on this particular document that we just move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, it's this Muratovic person who is talking in the paragraph starting with "Herceg-Bosna is constantly finding new forms." This is Mr. Muratovic saying this, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It appears to be so, Your Honour. It is quoted in the article, and I put that proposition to the witness, which he can agree with or disagree with. Everybody in the courtroom certainly has the document. And the report itself, Your Honour, in terms of -- the lack of translation is one issue and that will certainly have to be corrected, but apart from that, this is absolutely no different from the hundreds of other media articles that the Chamber has seen in the last two and a half years. So I think that that's the point of putting it to the witness, to ask him if that was continued -- if these facts were true. He's expressed his disagreement with some of this, and the Chamber's heard his testimony. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would just ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would just ask my colleague to be a little more careful. He's not just -- he's not quoting the text. He's quoting an individual that's in the text. And if you go back to the question, he never gives notice to the gentleman that this is what Mr. Muratovic is claiming. I do think that it is fair to -- for the witness to know who it is that is making this accusation or assertion, and it's within that context that the answer can be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, we've already mentioned this at length. You know my answer very well. You know that the media, when they quote someone, you know, they put it in quotes, and this sentence is in quotes. And then we have Muratovic says or says Mr. Muratovic. So we know it's a quote. And Mr. Tomic seemingly was also interviewed, because he's also mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, he doesn't have the original version. That's -- that was my point. Unless we're saying that some witnesses, if they can plough through English, good or bad, they should just look at the English text. In this instance Mr. -- Mr. Scott indicated that he would read from the text because we didn't have the original. Fair enough. But if we go that route then at least we should go the extra step and say so-and-so claims the following. That's all I'm saying. If he had the original, fair enough. Then he would obviously look at the original and then he could say. That's my point. I'm not trying to obstruct or to deny the gentleman the opportunity to pose the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm going on, anyway, and on that point I understand Mr. Karnavas's point since the witness doesn't have it in front of him. If I had read the full passage he would have had more information, so on that point I think there's some merit to what's been said. But in any event, I think the witness knows the issue. He knows the situation. He's able to address it and he has addressed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness wanted to answer. You can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I've just looked at the whole text. Look at the second paragraph on the same page starting with "Dr. Nikola Grabovac." I would kindly ask you to read this paragraph, and you will see that this was the position that I held at the time and that I'm sharing with you now. Mr. Grabovac quoted me because he was the only person there at the meeting that was being held. We were in favour of the functioning of the federation. However, we insisted on establishing institutions that would be treated as federal institutions. Every day Bosniak side would accuse us because they wanted Herceg-Bosna to stop functioning and for us to be incorporated within the system of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was contrary to the Washington Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, during the time that you were the Minister of Finance of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and, as you've told us, the Finance Minister for the federation and, if I understand correctly, at least for a time Finance Minister of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you consider that you owed any sort of allegiance or duty to the Republic of Croatia during that time in any of those positions?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the Minister of Finance in the government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina where I represented the Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was my duty. And our task was to establish federal institutions and the implementation of the Washington Agreement.
