utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Witness, I've listen to you carefully. You were Minister of Finance of the federation. I thought that you were the Ministry of Finance -- Minister of Finance, because you're extremely competent in this area and you were appointed to this position, but you have added that you represented the Croats. So I can't really understand this. A person is Minister of Finance because he's competent, be it whether he's a Croat, a Serb, or a Muslim, or are we Minister of Finance because we represent the Croats here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the distribution of functions in the government after the Washington Agreement the position of the Finance Minister was given to a Croat, i.e., a person of Croatian origin. Of course that person had to be competent, but he also had to be Croat. That was the political agreement of the signatories of the Washington Agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you can turn in your binder to -- I'll tell you the number in just -- the binder in a moment. P 08818. It should be in binder number 2. P 08818. And this is a record of a meeting with President Tudjman on the 7th of February, 1998. And can you tell us as we begin looking at this document what, if any, position Mr. Prlic held in any part of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the federation at that time?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that at the time he was the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you turn to page 11, please, of this transcript. There's one part that I would like to ask you about. Starting at about the middle -- above the middle of page 11, continuing over to the top of page 12, we have this statement attributed to Mr. Prlic, and I'll start with the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. These pages are missing from the Croatian version. I have 7 and then I have 14, nothing in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps we can assist you if that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The same here, Mr. Scott. We have --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: 15 -- no, 8 and then 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, obviously, Your Honour, my apologies, if there's been an error. If we can work in the e-court then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, it should be available to you. You should be able to see it on the screen in both English or certainly Croatian in a moment. If you go back to page 11, please. Okay. Thanks very much. Mr. Prlic says in the third paragraph under his intervention: "Mr. President, last year the surplus between Croatia and us was 400 million marks." I note that we're still talking in German marks. "It is an enormous amount; goods that cannot be sold in any other market, only Croatia starts off without the custom duty. For a year and a half they were trying to put an end to it. Only thanks to Tomic and me has it not been stopped yet. "In a couple of days the united customs zone will start functioning in Bosnia and Herzegovina ... control, and we will not be able to oppose that. We are facing a threat, because if the Republika Srpska is inside, it means that Yugoslavia is inside as well. "In that regard, I think that this matter is not discussed here enough. As regards to the economy, it is extremely important; 400 million marks of surplus are very important to Croatia." Sir, when Mr. Prlic and you were acting in your official positions on behalf of the federation and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you consider that you were supposed to be acting in their best interests or in the best interests of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were supposed to protect the interests of Bosnia and Herzegovina, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. Prlic says here that in terms of this favourable treatment Croatia was receiving, he says: "For a year and a half they were trying to put an end to it. Only thanks to Tomic and me has it not been stopped yet." It was the other authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina were trying to put a stop to this arrangement; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Bosniak side tried to stop that unilaterally, without passing documents that had been envisaged by the Washington Agreement. According to the Washington Agreement, the documents of the then existing administrative arrangements of Herceg-Bosna would be in effect until the moment either federal or the republican documents were passed. Since we wanted new institutions and new agreements to be established, the result was as Mr. Prlic put it. We did not fight for Croatia. We fought for the Washington Agreement to be implemented in the form in which it was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you again that Herceg-Bosna and the HDZ throughout this time period was doing everything possible to obstruct the Washington Agreement, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if we can go to -- sir, if we can go to the question of the use of the term "Bosnia and Herzegovina" in fact on various documents or insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Scott. The witness answered your question, which is an important question since you say that he was obstructing the Washington Agreements. The witness says no, and then you move on to something else. It might have been interesting to hear the witness on this point, why he wasn't standing in the way of the Washington agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I leave the witness in your hands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the signing of the Washington Agreement, we went to Sarajevo with other colleagues. We risked our lives on Igman, and when passing -- and we passed through the tunnel to get into Sarajevo. War was still raging there. This isn't obstruction. This demonstrates one's intention to do one's job as specified in the Washington Agreement, namely the construction of new institutions from the Central Bank to new customs administration of the federation, to the federation budget. We insisted on this. At that time the media in Sarajevo circulated a story according to which we were acting in an obstructive way, because it was impossible to perform our duties as ministers in the government of the federation of the republic because we were in Sarajevo and we had no authority in the territory under the control of the HVO. Well, we stated that as a precondition for our future work it would be necessary in that transitional period to have people who were in Sarajevo who were ministers in Herceg-Bosna. We were again appointed as ministers in Herceg-Bosna, but why? So that the process of implementing the Washington Agreement and of creating institutions could be carried out in a competent way by those who were familiar with the situation on the ground. The problem is that the media and those in favour of the government, as stated in these documents, and that meant pro-Bosniak at the time, the problem was that they kept circulating a story according to which we were seizing revenue in the territory of Herceg-Bosna. Duty was never imposed on goods and were being sent to territory under the control of the ABiH. And there was a continual conflict of this kind, continual clash, but it wasn't possible for us to clarify the situation through the media, to explain what was at stake. And for this reason and other for reasons I claim that we didn't obstruct anything. We tried to implement what had been stated in the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With this in mind, why didn't you say that all the custom duties levied by the -- by the Herceg-Bosna would be paid into the government of the federation? Why was this never said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, look, the agreement between the minister who was in the government of the republic and myself, and at the time I was a deputy in Herceg-Bosna, this was after Washington, the agreement was during the transitional period and up until the time federal institutions were established, new institutions, these were new institutions, there was no budget I could pay money into, this was the budget of that BH republic whose new constitution hadn't yet taken force. So we can't pay money that is the federation's money into the budget republic -- the republican budget. It was a game and there was pressure for us to pay this money into the republic's budget. The federation shouldn't even have to be established, because -- as I have already said in the course of my testimony. The Bosniak side accepted all solutions as transitional solutions until a final state solution. It wanted to keep things in its hands until this issue was dealt with. We wanted part of -- we wanted a role in the power in accordance with the Washington Agreement. And that's why we had the agreement on bringing to life the federation, and this was before Dayton. In this agreement the government of the federation was separated from the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this is when the process actually took off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, didn't -- and continuing the same issue, didn't the international community and a number of non-governmental organisations throughout this period repeatedly, repeatedly find the HVO, the HDZ, Herceg-Bosna being complete obstructionists to both Washington and Dayton? You do remember that? You certainty were aware that report after report was coming out at the time saying these things.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were reports. The question is who discussed these reports with those people. The people who spoke to me never conveyed such a position in any reports. I had contact with people from the World Bank, from the IMF, from the European bank, and finally under their supervision we -- we established those federal institutions, as I said. There was a group of 10 or 12 of us in Sarajevo at the time. We didn't have infrastructure of our own. We had no communications, and we were being supervised by Sarajevo departments. Well, in such a situation what could we have done? How could we have explained to someone what was being done when people from ministries said that they were from federal ministries, which was not at all the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you please --

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I sa that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... P 10279. P 10279. That's the third binder, first document in the third -- binder number 3. And this is a document that's previously been admitted. In line with what you've said in the last few moments, I'd like to show it to you. Sir, this is part of a report that was issued in April 2000 by the International Crisis Group, which I believe is an extremely reputable international organisation. If you look at the first page, page 1, I will read it -- some of the passages to you. It starts out the introduction: "Mostar is a city divided." Going to the end of that first paragraph: "Since the war, the Bosnian Croat HDZ, Croatian democratic party, has actively opposed all efforts, both figurative and literal, at bridge building." Skipping to the third paragraph: "In terms of achieving, actually achieving reunification, international community and EU efforts have failed. After six years of international community assistance and supervision the administration, economy, infrastructure, education, police, and legal systems of Mostar remain sharply divided along ethnic lines. The only real achievement to date in Mostar has been freedom of movement. The greatest indication of the international community's failure today has been the persistent and largely unchallenged obstruction by the HDZ implementing property laws and refugee return." Going to the next paragraph: "Since 1994, the HDZ leadership, in cooperation with the HDIDRDA, which the Chamber heard about several weeks ago from another witness, and powerful Herzegovinian economic interest has repeatedly blocked not only international community efforts to reunite Mostar but also the implementation of the federation agreement and the Dayton peace agreement." Going over to page 2, section A, HDZ Obstruction: "Since signing the first agreement in Geneva in 1994, the ruling Croat political party, the HDZ, has prevented all progress by blatantly obstructing over 30 subsequent agreements ... the HDZ has carried out a policy of maintaining a divided city, canton and federation, obstructing all agreements at various official levels and at different times, engaging in a continuous game of good cop-bad cop with the international community." Now, I don't think I need to read more. That was the common consensus among the international community throughout this time period, was it not, leading in fact to various actions being taken by the office of High Representative against the senior leadership of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have an objection. The Prosecutor has said that this is the assessment of the international community. We don't know what the ECG group is. First of all we should know what ECG means. We can't just say that it's the international community. This is very abstract. Secondly, it's a document from the April 2002. As far as I can remember, the witness was a mayor in Mostar, if I remember correctly, but this line of questioning that has been pursued for over an hour, half an hour now, well, as far as I know, and I think I do know, the time-frame of the indictment is until the Dayton agreement -- the Washington Agreement. I apologise. So why are we now dealing with events in Bosnia and Herzegovina after the signing of the Washington Agreement -- or, rather, after the time-frame covered by the indictment? And thirdly, if this is what we're dealing with, well, then we have to deal with this up to this very day, because some of these problems, as far as I know, given the supervision law that we have about it, well, some of these problems are still present today. So this line of questioning is not relevant. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, do you wish to respond? But you have responded a few weeks ago when you said that as far as you were concerned, the JCE still prevailed after the Washington agreement. Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, in this sense, and that is that we -- what the Prosecution's case is and the Chamber may ultimately agree or disagree, but it's the Prosecution case that Herceg-Bosna represented a long-term project that did not end with Washington or Dayton, and the reason that's relevant is because among -- among other things is because the Defence has repeatedly said it was temporary, it was provisional, it wouldn't last after the war, and this witness -- the further answer is this witness himself has this afternoon said everything that the Bosnian Croats and the HDZ was trying to do to implement the Washington Agreement and everything that was being done and they were holding out because they didn't want to organise this institution or they didn't want to do this or they couldn't pay the customs revenue in to them yet because of some reason. So he's made all of this, Your Honour, directly relevant, and I'm challenging his testimony on that point. And I do submit that this is only one document, but again we have a very educated man in front us who has been a senior government official. He must have known. I assume he was reading the newspapers at the time. He was meeting with senior government officials. He must have known. He must have known that these were issues and allegations that were being brought against the HDZ almost every day. Now, if he wasn't aware of that and he wasn't following, watching the news, watching the television or reading the newspaper or watching CNN, then maybe he didn't know but I submit to you that he did, and he -- he has every capable means of responding to my questions that I put to him several times this afternoon, "Sir, isn't it true that the H -- the Herceg-Bosna that continued to exist and the HDZ were doing everything possible to obstruct the Washington Agreement?" And several times he said no. This exhibit is directly relevant to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave I would like to respond. Unless I misheard something, but I think I heard this correctly and I've been following the transcript, the Prosecution is now claiming before this Tribunal that joint criminal enterprise, and we know what we're talking about, the enterprise covered in the indictment, was a long-term project and did not come to an end with the Washington or Dayton agreement. I can't understand this in any other way. I can only take it to be an amendment to the indictment. I have already raised this objection, and you, the Chamber, tried to persuade me that the Prosecution wasn't amending the indictment. But if the Prosecution is making such a claim when this comes to investigating the circumstances and events, and this is outside the scope of the indictment, well, in such a case the only possible explanation is that the Prosecution is thereby amending or changing the indictment. And one other thing I would like to add, I didn't mention it because I wanted to be brief, the Prosecution is again being given a certain right. The Prosecution is not asking whether it could put questions outside the scope of examination-in-chief. I'd like to remind you of Rule 19(H)(i), you can go beyond the scope, but one has to explain why. If the explanation is that one wants to go beyond the scope of examination-in-chief because the claim that -- because of the claim that the joint criminal enterprise is a long-term project, well, then the Prosecution has to say that and say why this is his opinion and also say whether he is amending the amendment. The Prlic Defence case is coming to its end. Five other Defence teams have to start their cases. We can't define the limits of our defence case if in a certain sense, the implication is that the time-frame of the indictment is being broadened. That is my objection and I would like it to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Based on -- based on what I heard, it would appear now that it is an expanded indictment, and I certainly would ask at least with the conclusion of this witness's testimony that we be given additional time to, one, do further investigation and, two, additional time to put on a case. Recently I just read comments made by the supervisor in Brcko district, who happens to be an American ambassador who talks about the Bosniaks continuing their project for a unitary state, the Serbs wanting -- Republika Srpska wanting to break away because in part of this unitary project where the Croats are still interested in having a third entity in BiH. Now, if we are going to allow the Prosecutor to talk about 2000 and thereafter, then we must be given an opportunity to now discuss what is going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina even today while there are discussions on amending the constitution, because one of -- one of the abusers of the Dayton Peace Accord has been indeed the international community, none other than the office of the High Representative where they're imposing laws, violating the letter and spirit of the Dayton Accords and the annexes which are the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the constitution of the federation, the constitution of the Republika Srpska, and even the final award which created the Brcko district. So if we're going to go into this area and if you're going to allow this kind of questioning, then it is an acknowledgement by the Bench that it is indeed going to consider this information and this evidence, that it is allowing the Prosecution even at this late stage of the game to expand the indictment, and therefore we need to take certain actions on our part. We need to defend against this. And I -- as I take it based on the question that you posed, Mr. President, and the answer that we got, that indeed the indictment has been amended to include all these other things. So I do think that maybe this is not the time to argue this, but we need to have a session to figure out what is it are we supposed to defend against? Is it the indictment, the four corners of this -- of this mega document, or are we going to go beyond? We need to know. Especially I need to know because if I knew that I was going to go into post-Dayton implementation 2000 plus, then obviously be would be prepared for that to put on a case, but I have been limited and my time has been limited based on the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I don't have the indictment before me but if I remember correctly from memory, in the indictment it is stated that there is a JCE was started before, comma, from such a day to such a date and afterwards. We have the words "before" and "after." This is in the indictment, so read the indictment again. There is a date that is mentioned as a start date and an end date -- it has a start date. You have the words "before" and "after." So read the indictment again. I don't have it before me. Mr. Scott has already said this, and the Trial Chamber has said that it would assess this time period in light of the material adduced. Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Before I give the floor to Mr. Praljak, I would like to read [no interpretation ... approximately and after -- various people, so on and so forth. Let me read it again. This hasn't been recorded on the transcript. Paragraph 15: "From on or before the 18th of November, 1991, to about April 1994 and thereafter," comma, so we are talking about the period before the 18th of November, 1991, and April, 1994. What we talk about from on or before and about April 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like a brief break so that I can consult my lawyer. I didn't believe I would have to listen to an indictment of a political nature again, which is what I had to do in Communist Yugoslavia from the middle ages to the present day, lasts from the middle ages to the present day. If the HZ HB obstructed anything after the Dayton agreement, then you have to ask yourselves why the Americans created Republika Srpska after everything it had done, so what is at stake here is that the political right of those who are powerful is transformed into someone's right at court. This is just a display of the imperial power of the Prosecutor who isn't even acting in accordance with the laws of this Tribunal. I am requesting that we have a break so that I can examine how I proceed. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This is an important issue that we've had before, and maybe it would be good if -- if the Chamber sat on it and answered the questions that have been raised on both sides. My suggestion is that we postpone this for at least next week, because we have this witness who is an important witness, as the Defence rightly has argued, and whom we cannot keep into tomorrow, and I think we should really use the time now to take advantage of everything this witness can tell us. I wonder whether my colleagues agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Scott showed you this document, which is a document prepared by the ECJ. According to Mr. Scott this international crisis group is a well -- very well-known group. I had never heard about it before. And the International Crisis Group talks about a number of issues. What is your answer to this? Mr. Kovacic, please sit down. My colleague has said that this issue will be discussed next week, but for the time being the witness needs to finish his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... agree. I don't really want to take the floor but I think my client has the right to ask for a brief pause to consult his Defence regardless of Mr. Trechsel's suggestion and I personally except the suggestion. I believe that the Chamber should take a decision, it would be good for the Chamber to take a decision. Perhaps you can give us a short break nor or perhaps later. It's for you to decide, naturally.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will be able to talk to Mr. Praljak during the break. The Bench would like to say that when the court is back in session this question will not be addressed. However, the witness will have to respond and provide an answer in light of the document that's been shown to him by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is half past 5.00. Mr. Scott, you have used up five hours and four minutes so far. How much longer do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope to use less than my allotted time, but I'm certainly not counting on doing substantially less than the eight hours and seven minutes that Mr. Karnavas has used. I may do better, but I may not. I can't commit to doing better than that, although I hope to. But Mr. Karnavas -- well, I mean that quite sincerely, Your Honour. I spent a considerable matter of time since yesterday cutting my outline substantially, but at the same time Mr. Karnavas got his time, and I expect to use the same amount of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I'm putting to question to you, because you know that there is no hearing schedule tomorrow because the Krajisnik case is going to sit all day. There might be an another problem. But that means that this witness may have to come back another time. Let me ask Mr. Tomic a question. Is there a possibility for you to come back, to return at some point in time? We still have an hour and a half to go, but he will not have -- the Prosecutor will not have been finished with his eight hours, and Mr. Karnavas might have additional questions. He's suggesting that he will probably need two hours, two additional hours. So you will have to return at one point in time. There's no other way around. So it's up to you, Mr. Witness. We might have a spot -- a slot for you for your return. There will be a couple weeks where we have nothing, notably the first week in December. I'm talking out of memory. So maybe you could return for the first week of December, or the second week of December. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Next week we have a witness, but the following week, the 17th, we don't. We don't have any witnesses. So that would be the 17th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. There's an additional slot that just opened up, November 17th. So you could come back on November 17th. It might take two days at most, I mean, at most, worst case scenario. There's no other way around. I know that you are having a company. This creates great problems for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also have some family commitments, so I wouldn't be able to tell you off-the-cuff which slots are available to me because I have some family travel planned, also some business travel planned. There are some things pending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we have scheduled this for November 17th. Next week we have a witness scheduled, and then we have an open slot, November 17th. That could be very -- that could be possible for you. So check with your wife, see maybe how to manage this, but rest assured, now we have an hour and 15 minutes left for today. Mr. Scott will thus have two more hours to finish his cross-examination. Mr. Karnavas needs two additional hours for redirect, but that four hours means two days, so that's Monday to Tuesday at most. Mr. Scott, let's waste no additional time and please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Ken, if you -- [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't wish to take any more of your time. However, I've looked at the record, and I'm not sure about your decision. His Honour Judge Trechsel proposed that this very important issue be put on a -- on the agenda of a special session perhaps next week, to have a discussion, because obviously we are hard pressed for time. The witness is here. I don't want to take the witness's time or the Court's valuable time. However, I believe that the temporal framework of the indictment has to be discussed and the Trial Chamber has to give us their opinion, otherwise we are in the dark. If this is your decision according to what Mr. -- His Honour Judge Trechsel said that we will have a special date dedicated to that, then we will agree to that. Otherwise, this kind of a cross-examination will be considered a pure politicising and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will discuss this among ourselves, and we'll keep you informed on Monday at 2.15. We'll tell you whether there will be a special hearing just on this case -- on this problem that will be organised or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, some -- some minutes ago now we -- I was asking you -- going to the question of during your direct examination, and again this arises in particular in connection with customs and borders, border controls, and there was some questioning about what was on the badge, I think, and what was on the identity card use by the officers, and I think there was something to the effect saying that there was something of the words "Bosnia-Herzegovina" at least on some of those items, whether it was on the identity card or the badge or something, but I do note that you testified about this last Tuesday. Sir, isn't it correct that those such words as "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina" were on Herceg-Bosna stationary and on various documentation really primarily for appearance's sake? It's what the Judges have heard in this case as the two-track policy. On one hand you profess allegiance and loyalty to Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the other hand, on the second track, there's actually a different agenda. And that was the nature of that language in such items, wasn't it? It was for appearance's sake.

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We adopted republican decrees. Our stamp featured the title of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Our headings, the logo of our letters featured that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it correct that again those words and things like that were added to this documentation for political reasons and in fact because that was the guidance given to the HVO from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that guideline. I know that the first documents that I drafted featured the name of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the territory of the HZ HB during the war and under the immediate threat of war temporary nature. This was my starting guideline, and this is the principle that guided me when I establish the system of finance as a part of the HZ HB system.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you will please turn in the Defence binder to 2D 01262. It will be again in the smaller fourth, or Defence, binder, so to speak. 2D 01262. Sir, this is the record that -- I think we've looked at it earlier in the course of your testimony, but it's the record of a meeting of the of HZ HB Presidency on the 17th of October of 1992. Apparently the meeting was presided over by Dario Kordic, and we see a number of the people who were found to be present, including Bozo Rajic, president of the HVO HZ HB Jadranko Prlic, Department For Finances Neven Tomic, excuse me, department for justice and administration Zoran Buntic, et cetera. Now, if I can please direct your attention to the record of this meeting, and it will be page 14 of the English version. And if you can find it, sir. It will be under -- you will find on the page there are some markings 11 -- 9, 10, 11. And if you find one that's for item number 11, "Proposition of the directive on administrative taxes." That's not what I'm going to direct you to, but I'm just -- I'm trying to assist you in terms of finding your way through the document. Do you see that? Agenda item 11, "Proposition of the directive on administrative taxes." After that is: "Neven Tomic - Head of Department for Finances," if that again helps you find it. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if you'll go above the item 11 about four or five paragraphs you will find a paragraph that starts with these words: "President Mate Boban posed a question why RBiH appears in all HZ HB acts, and Mr. Buntic gave explanation to this question by emphasizing that this was necessary from political reasons and because Zagreb insisted on this in given moment." And that was the case; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object at this point, Your Honour. Mr. Buntic was here. The opportunity to have raised this issue in putting the case to the witness would have been at that point in time, not to this particular witness. He's now being asked to validate or speculate as to another witness's testimony. So there's a clear rule that you have to put to -- your case to the witness, and that's exactly the reason why we have this rule. We don't have it in the States, but it is something that we've inherited in this -- in this Tribunal from the British and the Australian system.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this witness -- Your Honours, this witness was -- this witness was at the meeting. We just saw that. And the -- he has made in particular this particular section relevant by his direct testimony in which he talked about -- he was asked and he gave answers to what was on the documentation, what -- what was on the badges, et cetera, et cetera. So it's directly relevant to the testimony of this witness. And he was at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness attended the meeting, so we can all -- we can at least ask the witness what he thinks of someone else's answer, an answer given by someone else in this meeting. But it is true, Mr. Karnavas, this question should have been put to Mr. Buntic directly. You're also right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, wasn't that the advice that was put forward at the meeting on the 19th of October, that the reason all these -- the reason this was being done was for the reasons -- excuse me, the 17th of October, for the reasons stated here?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I understood political reasons was the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We were just a temporary solution within the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Zagreb insisted on that because it had recognised the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's the way I understood the situation, and I continued drafting my documents in the way I did in the month of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to go to the topic of the language of the referendum in February -- or, yes, in February 1992. You were asked some questions about what your -- what the Croat desired position was in terms of the organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Last Thursday you testified if that was your position essentially that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be organised in the manner of having three ethnic units. Mr. Tomic said yes. When asked whether BiH should have been set up "comprising several constituent units and each of these constituent units should have been set up in such a way that criteria ethnicity was taken into account." And you talked about that in reference to the referendum language. And isn't it not correct, sir, that the actual language desired by the -- a majority of the HDZ was a very different question than the one that was actually on the referendum? You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the referendum question. The Croatian side adopted the referendum, adopted Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was outlined at that moment that the organisation of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina should be organised in a different way for which the Croats believed that it could protect their own possession in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can please go to Exhibit P 00117, which will be in the first binder. P 00117. In this record of another -- a meeting of the HDZ Central Board, HZ BiH central board on February 9, 1992, and under conclusions if you will find the item number 3, a referendum on a sovereign independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you recall, sir, that the HDZ leadership or some of them at least were unhappy with the formulation of the referendum question as it was to be about on the ballot a few weeks later? That existing language says something to this effect, and we can see it further below on that same page: "Are you in favour of a sovereign and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, a state of equal citizens and peoples, Croats, Muslims, Serbs, and other peoples who live in it?" And if you look above that, sir, do you recall that the language desired by the HD -- the alternative language desired by the HDZ was: "Are you in favour of a sovereign and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, a joint state of the constitutive and sovereign Croatian, Muslim, and Serbian peoples in their ethnic areas (cantons)?" That was the question -- that was the form of the referendum that the HDZ leadership wanted; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as stated there would that -- would you have agreed? Was that also your position at that time? Bosnia and Herzegovina should be set up on the basis of three ethnic units?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina is a state inhabited by three equal peoples, and the organisation of the state should have been such to make sure that all the three peoples are able to exercise their rights. At that moment one couldn't speak about the final model, and that is why the referendum question did not include the addition that had been proposed by the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And continuing on with your testimony, was it -- you essentially, as I take it, and I understand your testimony and you can correct me, you were essentially against an integrated society in the former Yugoslavia in the sense that the notion -- in any sense that the notion of persons who were Croats, Serbs, or Muslims would go away or become less significant. You were against that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you testified last week on Thursday. You said it was your personal opinion that in the Communist system over a long period of time had tried to build an artificial nation, an artificial nation, the Yugoslav nation, and eliminating other nations or ethnic groups in the process. In other words, the number of Croats, Serbs, and Muslims would decrease at the expense of the Yugoslavs, whose numbers would rise. And you were against that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've explained the situation, for example, in Mostar and how it transpired. I didn't say whether I was in favour or against. I just explained the situation as it prevailed at the moment after the elections in Mostar, and I hope that that's been recorded properly. I did not voice my opinion on any of the variants because that was not a question that I was supposed to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'm doing asking you now, sir. Is that your view, and was that the view that you endorsed at the time in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, what view, Your Honours? You have constituent peoples that live in Yugoslavia. So if you are a Slovenian or a Croatian or a Serbian. Now, is the question is that they should abandon their heritage to become Yugoslavs? Is that the question? The question is unclear as is stated, and perhaps my learned friend doesn't understand what a constituent person is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps I -- perhaps I do, Mr. Karnavas. Perhaps I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, could you reformulate your question, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- so that it is clear? The witness said that the question was not put to him that way. So please reformulate your question, and if he can answer he will answer, and if he can't, he won't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was simply quoting the witness's testimony back to him as a basis for my question. Last Thursday he testified as follows: "My personal opinion is that the Communist system over a long period of time tried to build an artificial nation, the Yugoslav nation, and eliminating, eliminating, other nations or ethnic groups in the process. In other words, the number of Croats, Serbs, and Muslims would decrease at the expense of the Yugoslavs whose numbers would rise." And based on that testimony under oath I asked him did that reflect his view, and he was -- to the extent that he was against an integrated society, to the extent that those notions, those ethnic notions would become less significant and people might think of themselves as -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, and I think this is the problem that's causing some concern here, is that the question he's asking -- the question he's asking, whether he is willing to abandon his national heritage in order -- that's what it is, Judge Trechsel. I mean, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you point to the text precisely where that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Based on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- abandonment of national heritage is referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, because -- because in order to become a Yugoslav, you have to stop being a Croat or a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You are interpreting this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. But that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You're interpreting it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Where does it speak of the heritage and of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's a general view of a political development and the witness can say whether he approved of such a development or whether he rejected it. It is not even laden with any value judgement. One might then say he was right this way or he might even be equally right. It's just his opinion. I for one am not quite sure what the relevance of the answer is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, that's my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There -- there maybe we can agree, but I think there is no harm done if he simply answers the question as it was put.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this question gives rise to some passion, as you have noticed. Mr. Coric is on his feet. Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Prosecutor tried to accuse this witness here, because he opted to be against eliminating three nations, the Serbs, Muslims, and the Croats in the former Yugoslavia and to have them become Yugoslavs at one point in time in a given year, and he also draws a parallel and says that this witness is against the multi-ethnic life of these peoples. If one continues to pursue this route, well, the elimination of three peoples is tantamount to pure and simple Fascism. This is pure and simple Fascism in the Tribunal here and the Prosecution is giving us a subdued version of this from day to day, from hour to hour. And what I wanted to say -- and Judge Trechsel, you can interrupt me as much as you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. Coric. I don't think that the Prosecutor wishes to put his question in a Fascist light, that there is a Fascist connotation to his question. Before you step in, I think it would be better to listen to what the witness is about to say because the question is put to him. If he is outraged, he will say what you have just said, but maybe he understood the question differently. I'm trying to understand the question, and I'm waiting for the answer. Mr. Coric, wait for him to answer, and if necessary you can take the floor again afterwards. Witness, you have understood what the Prosecutor told you. You have heard what Mr. Coric has just said, what Mr. Karnavas has said, what Mr. Praljak, who is on his feet, also might have to say. Do you wish to answer or would you like the Prosecutor to phrase his question again? Either you haven't understood the question, or maybe you understood it too well. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to answer the question. This question was in response to a Defence question in which I was asked about my opinion relating to the situation that prevailed in Yugoslavia and relating to the break-up and so on and so forth. I expressed my opinion with regard to that matter, and I didn't state what my position is. I said I personally think that this happened for such-and-such a reason. I was a Croat at the time of Yugoslavia, and I performed my duties as a Croat, and I had nothing against Serbs or Muslims, or Yugoslavs for that matter. That was a matter for people to decide about, a matter of their personal opinion. But I was discussing the process and how it ended. That's what I did when I was discussing assemblies in Mostar for electoral purposes and when I said that SDS, HDZ, and SDA groupings and the two parties that gathered Yugoslavs, I said that they were viewed by an equal amount of people, but at the elections one noted that people made their decisions on national lines. The Yugoslavs either decided not to be Yugoslavs anymore or forgot that they were Yugoslavs. And to this very day I believe that if someone still believes that he or she is a Yugoslav, well, that's a matter of their personal opinion. But I was saying that in my opinion this is one the reasons for which Yugoslavia broke up, because it is obvious that the policies pursued in this respect were not fruitful. The policies were not fruitful because the Yugoslav nation did not become an element allowing one to implement what the policies advocated at the time. If I have understood the question correctly, that would be my answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you. I would only like to make the following comment: As far as I know, and of course I stand to be corrected, the issue of being a Yugoslav or not had been included in -- on two occasions in -- actually when the statistics had been drawn up, if I am not quite -- if I am sure. Then I would say that in 1990 last time, and before probably around 1980 when the issue of being Yugoslav had come up. Now as far as also I know, there had been mainly people of -- with mixed marriages, and being Hungarian I also heard that vote in Vojvodina and other places some people had chosen being Yugoslav because of probably thinking that it might help them to get along with the majority nations, et cetera. So therefore I was a bit surprised when Mr. Coric mentioned that it was a Fascist thing, pure Fascism to ask the question. So as far as I know, in 1990 there was an increase among the people who had chosen as being Yugoslavs. Of course after this whole issue had been removed from the -- from these questions. And I heard very recently even in Bosnia and Herzegovina, lastly they have rejected to organise -- organise again a kind of statistical possibilities to -- probably because they do not want to go into any clashes or conflicts concerning the nationality issues. So that is why I believe that we have to calm down and to look into this issue as -- as it was raised during those decades and years and not to -- not to emphasise the -- in a way some kind of Fascist or whatever -- whatever kind of names for it, because I believe that it was not the situation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, the witness has answered your question in line with what he'd said previously. So this is very precise. I shall give you the floor back now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, so then having referred back to your testimony from last week and then looking at the language from the HDZ meeting in February 1992, I just want -- it brings us back full circle, and if you didn't say it before, I may ask you to say it again. Was it your position, your personal view in 1992 and 1993 that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be -- should be established and set up on the basis of three separate ethnic units? Whatever you want to call them, entities, republics, cantons. Was that your view or position?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you put the question in that way, my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you to look at Exhibit P 10698, which will be in the third binder. P 10698. Sir, this is a -- while people are still looking, let me say for the record this is a Reuters news article dated the 28th of October, 1992, and about the middle of that page there is a reference to Mr. Prlic. Above that it says: "In an attempt -- in an attempt to head off a carve-up of Bosnia by Serbs and Croats at the expense of the Muslims, Vance and Owen proposed a state with a bare minimum central government and some autonomous -- excuse me, some ten autonomous regions. "But Jadranko Prlic, president of the republic declared by Croats in the area of Bosnia they control told Reuters that the only way to achieve a stable solution was to have three national units whose parts need not be physically connected." Now, that sounds to me like three national units, national, I take it being here, national being Serb, Croat, and Muslim. So I asked you a question a few moments ago and your answer to me was, when I put it that way, your answer was no. Did you share the view stated here and attributed to Mr. Prlic, the only way to achieve a stable solution was to have three national units?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion is that that is not the only way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really ask you that, sir. I said did you -- do you agree what -- let me restate it then. Given what we've looked at in the last half hour or so, the statement of the referendum in which the Central Board of the HDZ voted in favour of a referendum formulation which called for the ethnic groups in their separate ethnic areas, I've now shown you this article giving comments concerning Mr. Prlic, and I think, sir, in all fairness, I made it pretty clear to you and there shouldn't be any basis for confusion. Was it your position in 1993 that the way that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be arranged was on the basis of three separate ethnic units? Now, you -- it's quite clear, my question and the documents I've shown you, sir. Was that your view?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, any solution that put an end to the Croats' fear and ensured that they had an equal footing in Bosnia and Herzegovina, any such solution would be an acceptable one, whether the solution amounted to having cantons or regions or republics. Any structure, the functioning of which would ensure that the three peoples would have a constituent status would be for me an acceptable structure, an acceptable solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The notion of the three separate units that's reflected in the HDZ formulation of the referendum and in the article that we looked at a moment ago, that was based on a view at the time, was it not, it was okay or better or ethnic groups to live in proximity to one another but not, as some might say, not on top of each other. Do you remember that kind of language and discussion being in the public dialogue at the time? "We can live next to each other but not on top of each other?"

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In public life in Bosnia and Herzegovina it was also possible to hear such statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can turn, please, in your binder, it should be in the first binder, Exhibit P 00108. Sir, this is a record of a meeting in the presidential offices in Zagreb on the 8th of January, 1992, which I believe the Chamber has seen before. If I can direct your attention -- and this is a meeting involving, among others, President Tudjman, the Croat from Bosnia-Herzegovina named Franjo Boras and a Bosnian Serb named Nikola Koljevic, and others, but if I can direct your attention, please, to page number 3 in that record where Mr. Koljevic starts talking, and he says: "Thank you, Mr. Boras. I think that we can somehow name - we all know what is involved - that we can somehow name the most general pacifications of Serbo-Croatian relations and the attempt at our agreement on a political solution in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have several things written down, but that would be a general common point." Let me skip to some of that language -- over some of that language, and if you can go over to page 4. And the page numbers should be the same in both the English and the Croatian versions of the document, so it should be on page 4. First when Mr. Boras says -- excuse me, Mr. Koljevic says: "First, allow me to say, turning to this political crisis of ours, that the people in the Serbian Democratic Party have nothing either against the creation of a Croatian state, or against Croatian political organising in the form in which it suits the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Had there been a little more historical luck and more communication, I think this could have happened earlier." If I can direct your attention to page number 7. Page number 7, the last paragraph beginning on that page. "We essentially proposed a tripartite community, essentially considering that these institutions which ought to be separate should be separate, and that common ones would be found. We thought that the three national communities should recognise that fact and not falsify it. Because three national communities exist and they should normally, if we wish to speak democratically, have all opportunities for normal national development and for normal neighbourly development, because what we say, we have the custom of saying nowadays - to live next to each other. But not on top of one another." Then if I can direct your attention, please, to page 42. President Tudjman comes back into the conversation on the top of page 42 and says: "Wherever national problems so conceived emerged as they did with us, that was resolved from World War I and World War II, that was brought to a conclusion by exchanges ..." "Koljevic: I just wanted to say that I think what you have said about the ultimate goal, that this would be the way." And Mr. Tudjman goes on to say: "I agree, but we have to know that the serious world -- that the serious world that is not involved in petty politics, I'm thinking of the international factor ..." et cetera. In the next paragraph it says, I'm just trying to save a couple of moments: "If what Mr. Koljevic just said exists, if such agreement exists on the level of the Serbian party -- or part, then there will be - I must say that in the initial talks before this terrible war, Milosevic was very inclined towards such a solution. He told the leaders in Bosnia, the leaders of this Serbian policy in Bosnia, that we can count on having such partners, and then this terrible war broke out." That was the sentiment that was being expressed at the time not only in the presidential offices of President Tudjman between Franjo Boras and Mr. Koljevic and others, that was the sentiment expressed in the leadership of Herceg-Bosna and the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the form of the question. First of all, we have skipped over some 40 pages. The gentleman has not been given an opportunity to look at the entire exchange. We have cherry picked here and there, highlighted certain portions, and now we're putting a global question to the gentleman without giving him a fair opportunity under the rule of completeness to look at all of it and then if he wishes to pose that question or any other question, then it may be fair game. But to simply cherry pick and take out of context why was Boras there with Koljevic, how did he get there? Perhaps we should allow the gentleman to also hear Mr. Boras's testimony about this particular exchange and how it was that they went there at Mr. Koljevic's insistence that he had a proposal for Mr. Tudjman. So if we're going to do this, let's do it properly. I object to this line of questioning. I object to the form of the question. I think it's highly improper and it's highly unfair. The gentleman cannot be asked to opine on something without seeing the entire exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is -- this is the way that the Chamber has proceeded and the trial has proceeded for the last two and a half --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the way that the case has proceeded and the trial has been conducted for the past two and a half years, and the Chamber well knows that excerpts of documents have been used and various bits and pieces of documents have been used, in fact, at the Chamber's direction. And we don't go through every document. We don't tender the entire document sometimes and that's what the Chamber has told us to do. Now, if the Chamber wants to follow a different procedure at this point and would like to take a recess and give Mr. Tomic the time to read the entire transcript, then that's certainly within the Court's power, but this is no different than the way that the Chamber's conducted this trial for the last two and a half years. You know, Mr. Karnavas always says -- talks about cherry picking, but there is no way -- the entire courtroom knows that there would be no way that we would ever finish this trial if every time there was a 40-page document we read the entire 42 pages in the courtroom. So I think I proceeded properly. It arises from the -- excuse me. That's really not appropriate when there's commentary coming from the other side. They may disagree with me and I don't expect them to always agree with me but there should not be personal commentary being expressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, for what little it may add, for my part, I don't see a problem with the question put forward by my learned friend. It can't be possible that every time a document is put to a witness the entirety of the document is read by the witness. I mean, if a volume of the Encyclopedia Britannica is referred to it couldn't be right to expect the witness to go through all of those pages. Ordinarily, of course, any ambiguity or unfairness to one of the parties can be cured by re-examination and in my respectful submission the real thrust of the objection is not so much focused or premised on the question but the fact that because of the constraints of time areas that could be otherwise clarified in re-examination are somewhat curtailed because a party may not feel they have enough time to go into areas that have arisen in the course of cross-examination. So, Your Honours, I don't see for my part any objection with what my learned friend Mr. Scott is doing. I do think that there are sometimes issues about the time given for re-examination to clarify certain parts of documents that are put in in their entirety. Your Honours, I don't know if that assists but it's my observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. I think there might be a reasonable intermediate way. When parts of the document are skipped, and these documents of course are very well known to the Defence, if there is a point that was skipped that would have been relevant and the Defence puts that out and shows that there are -- is a passage which could change the assessment, I think then really a case has been made, but to blindly say that everything should be put, I agree with Mr. Khan. It really is not practicable and it doesn't make much sense either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I would agree on a very limited point and I will take exception with Mr. Khan, because this is a highly complex issue. Now, this is a very lengthy document. I don't have it -- I don't have the entirety before me. You do make a very logical, sensible, and appropriate observation, Judge Trechsel. However, when I'm only given parts of the document, how am I at this point to say point -- you know, this should be read and that should be read. That is part of the problem. If we had the entire transcript, then I could say, well, he should read this portion and that portion. So I entirely agree with you, and I'm not suggesting that we read all 46 pages, but it has to be put into some kind of context. And there is such a thing as the rule of completeness. If there is a previous section or a latter section that would be necessary for the witness to be aware of in order to give a meaningful answer, then they should be entitled to look at it, but the way this is -- the way Mr. Scott proceeded and the way the evidence I have in front of me, this document, it's virtually impossible for me to say he should also read page 11, page 22, section -- you know. I think I made my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, absolutely. I think again a solution might reside in that until the witness comes back, you look or you have someone look at this and then you counter-cherry pick, as it were, and present these cherries in redirect. But I think for the time being you should let Mr. Scott continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honour, two just very brief observations in response to the comments made and they'll be less than 30 seconds. Everyone knows the time issue is a serious concern for everyone in the case, including the Prosecution, and there is a wealth of material and a wealth of questions I would like to put to this witness concerning his testimony that I will never have a chance to because I don't have time to cover them. So the time issue is one that cuts in every direction. I've had to be very, very selective about what I can put to the witness given the time limitations that exist. Secondly, Your Honour, I can only observe and I'm sure everyone can appreciate it, if we put every presidential transcript in its entirety in the binders, instead of having four binders, you'd have about eight and I've already in the course of the day heard about three people dropped their binders. I'm sorry for that. It's an inconvenience for everyone, for everyone, but that's where we are, and putting in excerpts is just one practical way, unfortunately, of limiting the material. The entire document certainly is available to Mr. Karnavas. I understand that he may not have it in the courtroom. It's also available in e-court. And that's where we are. I'm sorry, I think I went more than 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I think the pending question to you some minutes ago was, the views expressed -- I put it to you, I'm putting my case to you, you may disagree, but the views expressed by Mr. Tudjman, Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Boras in this record that I've just read to you in part, which we got started on, if you remember I asked you -- do you remember hearing at the time there was a certain phrase or view being expressed in the public discourse at the time that, well, you know, we can live next to each other but not on top of each other, and indeed that was the very phrase that Mr. Koljevic used during this meeting? Was that not the sentiment held by the leadership of Herceg-Bosna and the HVO at this time?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my answer I said that in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina one could hear such positions even before you showed me this transcript. This was a thesis that Serb representatives pointed out and emphasised, which is similar to what Mr. Koljevic was saying in here. During this period which is January 1999, the HVO HZ HB did not exist, and as -- from the beginning of the work of the HVO HZ HB, not for a moment did such a concept exist in terms of ethnically pure units or maybe functioning of the HVO HZ HB as a unit of Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was not foreseen by any of our documents. The way we tried to organise a life in the territories under the control of the HVO, in the territory of the HZ HB, was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever become aware, sir, of such things as efforts of persons going into the various HVO detention camps or facilities and offering Muslim prisoners that they could be released if they signed loyalty oaths to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not seen any such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Wasn't it the case, sir, that various senior Herceg-Bosna HVO officials said that the desired solution was indeed to have three separate ethnic territories, again call them what you will, cantons, units, republics, mini states, that three separate entities, ethnic entities, but at the same time along for the possibility to have -- that there were a few Muslims in government and business that served as a good window dressing to make things look -- at least look a little more multi-ethnic? Wasn't that the view expressed by the HVO Herceg-Bosna leadership during this time period?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: HVO HZ HB organised life in the territory of the HZ HB within the framework of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was our primary task and goal. There were no positions to the effect of separation or eliminating people. In our work or at least to my knowledge, we did not implement any such thing. The concept that I adopted and my firm belief was that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be organised as agreed through the negotiations conducted under the auspices of the international community, and that was one of the reasons why we adopted the first agreement and we wanted to implement it immediately for that precise reason and we also wanted implement the Washington Agreement immediately. However, as I've already told you, my observations were what they were and I can corroborate my observations with a hundred of situations that I myself went through and experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go please --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, just a small intervention. The gentleman keeps using the word "area," and it keeps getting translated as "territory." Now, I know we've gone back and forth on this, but I just want to make sure that it's -- at least my record is being recorded that he's saying area as opposed to territory. Now, how you all want to interpret that, that's a decision I leave to -- to others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. It's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you could next turn to P 07876 which should be in the second binder. P 07876. Sir, this is a decision dated the 16th of February, 1994, over the name of Mr. Mate Boban, and naming the presidential council at the time of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and we see in Article II the members of that council, including such persons as Mr. Zubak, Mr. Bender, Mr. Markovic, number 6 Mr. Prlic, number 8 Mr. Coric, number 9 Mr. Akmadzic, and others. Then in III it names as the secretary of the presidential council a man named Vladislav Pogarcic. Did you know Mr. Pogarcic?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And prior to this time of being named as the secretary of the presidential council, what positions or functions had he held in Herceg-Bosna and/or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Pogarcic had arrived from Sarajevo. He was a member of the HVO side and then he arrived in Grude, and he was with the office of Mr. Boban. I don't know what he was at that particular moment, but I know that after the Washington he was the Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During the time when he was with Mr. Boban, would it be fair to characterise him as sometimes the term is used Chief of Staff or Chef de Cabinet? Was that Mr. Pogarcic's function for a time with Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was in his office, but I wouldn't be able to remember what his exact position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any particular dealings with Mr. Pogarcic during the time that he held these various positions or functioned in the ways that have been mentioned in the last few minutes?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not particularly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are not in the list of the members of the council, the presidential council. You are not mentioned, and I note that Mr. Prlic is just a member. The president being Mr. Kresimir Zubak. In terms of domestic policy in the republic, the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, how can you analyse this presidential council? Why is it that you're not a member? And second question, what is this meaning of Mr. Prlic being just a member and nothing more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time I was -- let me just see when this was. Yes, it was in February. I was the Deputy Minister of Finance, and I was not appointed to that council. And as for Mr. Prlic, he was appointed a member. My personal feeling is that Mr. Prlic was not -- let me put it this way, he did not enjoy Mr. Boban's trust. He was not a yes man, to put it that way. And the selection of Kresimir Zubak at that moment was just a way for Mr. Prlic's position to be reduced in size. That was on the part of Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which municipality did Mr. Zubak come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zubak came from the HVO Usora. Before the war it was part of the Doboj municipality, and after the Washington Agreement it became a municipality, that municipality of Usora.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This presidential council that was established in February 1994, in terms of the membership Mr. Prlic, although he was a member, listed only as a member of the presidential council, he continued to be prime minister; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. Jozo Martinovic was the Minister of Finance to whom you were his deputy; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. Coric by this time had taken what ministry position? Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. It's correct, is it not, sir, that this presidential council was formed at the time that Mr. Boban was in serious trouble with the international community and was essentially on his way out, and this presidential council was picked and approved in Zagreb; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who approved it. I can only see that the document was signed by Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Martinovic, the Minister of Finance, is it correct that he had been a senior finance official in the Croatian government before coming to Herceg-Bosna and taking this position?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before he arrived in Herceg-Bosna he was an advisor in the Privredna Banka of Zagreb, the commercial bank of Zagreb. And before that he was the Minister of Finance in the Republic of Croatia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When was he approximately the Minister of Finance in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he was a member of the first government in 1991, if my memory serves me right. When I first met him he was already an advisor in Privredna Banka, and I met him in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how long did he remain the Minister of Finance of Herceg-Bosna before returning to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't remember off-the-cuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, approximately 11 months later in January 1995 you took on the position of Minister of Finance; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I believe it was somebody else in the meantime, but I wouldn't be able to tell you who exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going back to Mr. Pogarcic, if I can ask you, please, to go to Exhibit P 08623, which will be in the second binder. P 08623.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this document was placed under seal, has been given a number but is under seal. Is that the case? Rule 70 seems to apply. We'll check this. I will ask my legal officer to check this, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think that it's one of the documents that has been Rule 70 at previous points in the Tribunal's life but has not necessarily continued to have that status. So it may be that it's one of those documents that can be used in the courtroom but not broadcast, provided outside the courtroom, if you will, whereas someone can come and collect it as has been the case with some other documents from other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is an interview with Mr. Pogarcic given on the 9th of December, 1995, to Slobodna Dalmacija, titled "Deputy Foreign Minister Opposes Integral States." "Interview with Vladislav Pogarcic, ethnic Croat deputy Foreign Minister of the republic and federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. An integral Bosnia is the least desirable solution for everybody. If people want it, it will be divided." And if I can ask you to go to the second page, presume in the translation as well, second page in the English version. And if you can find, sir, there's a point where the interviewer asks this question, if it will assist you, the question put to Mr. Pogarcic is: "Do you really think that the peaceful division of Bosnia is possible?" Do you have that? Do you have that passage, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEVEN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then Mr. Pogarcic responds -- it's a rather -- it's a bit of a long text but I think an important one. "Yes, in fact the possibility is the only clear result of these four years of war. Remember how Bosnia was described at the beginning of the war as a 'leopard skin?' Today, however, it is a country of three ethnic communities each having its own strictly delineated territory. This might be thought to be ugly. There are people who are even disgusted by this. But they should know that it is the result of the will of the population itself. The Serbs, Muslims, and Croats have ethnically cleansed territories wherever they could. Meanwhile, it must not be forgotten that the Pandora's box of ethnic cleansing was forced open by the Serbs, although the two other nations could not resist the temptation to take a look into it until they reduce the number -- the members of the other ethnic communities to 10 per cent or less of the total.
